chapterNote: Asaph's confession — the honest man's psalm about almost losing his faith, and Book Three's opening door. It begins with the creed stated ('surely God is good to Israel, to the pure in heart') and then immediately shows the creed nearly lost: 'but as for me, my feet had almost slipped.' The stumbling block was the oldest one: the prosperity of the wicked, drawn with a satirist's precision — deaths without pangs, bodies sleek, pride worn like a necklace and violence like a robe, eyes bulging from fatness, mouths laid claim to heaven while their tongues patrol the earth, asking 'how would God even know?' Against that, Asaph's clean heart seemed a bad investment: plagued all day, chastened every morning. The turn is a doorway: 'until I went into the sanctuary of God — then I understood their end.' Worship recalibrates the ledger: the wicked stand on slippery ground, gone in a moment like a dream at waking. And the psalm rises from theodicy to one of the summits of the whole Bible: I was a brute beast before You — YET I am continually with You; You hold my right hand, You guide me with Your counsel, and afterward You will receive me to glory. Whom have I in heaven but You? My flesh and my heart give out, but God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever. The last verse hands us the psalm's whole method: as for me, the nearness of God is my good.

1.text: A psalm of Asaph. Surely God is good to Israel, good to the pure in heart.
1.amp: A Psalm [mizmor] of Asaph [Asaph]. Truly ['Yet', akh, the KJV margin] God [Elohim] is good [tov] to Israel [Yisrael], even to such as are of a clean ['clean of heart', bar lebab, the KJV margin] heart.
1.notes: akh, 'surely / yet' — the little particle carries the whole drama: this is the conclusion stated FIRST, the verdict Asaph nearly lost and now nails to the door before telling how. bar lebab (H1249, H3824), the pure in heart, the very ones the Lord would later pronounce blessed (cf. Matthew 5:8).

2.text: But as for me — my feet had almost turned aside; my steps had all but poured out from under me.
2.amp: But as for me, my feet [regel] were almost [meat] gone [natah — turned aside]; my steps [ashur] had well nigh slipped [shaphak — been poured out].
2.notes: The confession right behind the creed: kimat, almost — faith's close call admitted in public. shaphak (H8210) is the pouring-verb: footing running out like spilled water. The Psalter's honesty here has steadied centuries of believers standing on the same ice.

3.text: For I was envious of the arrogant boasters when I kept seeing the peace and prosperity of the wicked.
3.amp: For I was envious [qana] at the foolish [halal — the boastful, the arrogant], when I saw [raah] the prosperity [shalom] of the wicked [rasha].
3.notes: qana (H7065) is the burning envy-zeal, and the trigger is exquisitely chosen: the rasha enjoying SHALOM (H7965) — the covenant blessing-word, apparently paid to the wrong accounts. The eye kept raah-ing, and the seeing became the slipping.

4.text: For they have no torments in their death, and their bodies are sleek and well-fed.
4.amp: For there are no bands [chartsubbot — pangs, torturing bonds] in their death [mavet]: but their strength ['fat', ul bari, the KJV margin] is firm.
4.notes: The observation starts at the deathbed, where accounts should settle — and even there the wicked seem exempt: no chartsubbot (H2784), no death-pangs, and the ul (H193), the body, plump to the end. Envy always studies a curated feed; the sanctuary will show the unedited footage.

5.text: They are not in the troubles common to man, and they are not struck with plagues like the rest of mankind.
5.amp: They are not in trouble [amal] as other men [enosh]; neither are they plagued [naga — struck] like other men [adam].
5.notes: The exemption clause, as it appears from outside: no share in the amal (H5999) of enosh, no naga (H5060) with adam. Asaph's data was real but partial — verse 18 will supply the missing column.

6.text: Therefore pride is their necklace, and violence wraps them like a garment.
6.amp: Therefore pride [gaavah] compasses them about as a chain [anaq — a necklace]: violence [chamas] covers [ataph] them as a garment [shith].
6.notes: Prosperity's wardrobe: gaavah (H1346) worn openly as jewelry — arrogance turned ornament — and chamas (H2555) draped like a robe. What ought to shame them, they accessorize with; unbroken ease dresses a man in his sins.

7.text: Their eyes bulge out from fatness; the imaginations of their heart spill over every limit.
7.amp: Their eyes [ayin] stand out [yatsa] with fatness [chelev]: they have more than heart could wish ['they pass the thoughts of the heart', abar maskiyyot lebab, the KJV margin].
7.notes: The portrait's grossest stroke: the ayin bulging from chelev (H2459), appetite made anatomy. The margin's reading is sharper still — their maskiyyot (H4906), the heart's imaginations, abar (H5674), overflow all banks: having everything, they fantasize past everything.

8.text: They mock, and they speak malice; from on high they talk of oppression as policy.
8.amp: They are corrupt [muq — they scoff], and speak [dabar] wickedly [ra] concerning oppression [osheq]: they speak loftily [marom — from the heights].
8.notes: osheq (H6233), extortion, discussed be-marom (H4791), from the heights — oppression planned in the tone of men reviewing a portfolio. muq (H4167), the scoffing: cruelty with a smirk is the finished form of unjudged ease.

9.text: They have set their mouth against the heavens, while their tongue struts through the earth.
9.amp: They set [shathah] their mouth [peh] against the heavens [shamayim], and their tongue [lashon] walks [halak] through the earth [eretz].
9.notes: Total jurisdiction claimed by one small organ: the peh annexing shamayim, the lashon on patrol through eretz — heaven legislated against, earth talked into line. James's world-of-iniquity tongue (cf. James 3:6) in its imperial phase.

10.text: So His people turn back here, and waters of a full cup are drained by them.
10.amp: Therefore his people [am] return [shub] hither: and waters [mayim] of a full [male] cup are wrung out [matsah — drained] to them.
10.notes: The bitterest data point: God's own am (H5971), watching the wicked thrive, shub (H7725) — drift back toward them — and drink the spectacle down to the dregs (matsah, H4680). Unanswered prosperity is evangelistic; it converts the watching faithful to envy.

11.text: And they say, 'How would God know? Is there really knowledge in the Most High?'
11.amp: And they say [amar], 'How does God [El] know [yada]? and is there knowledge [deah] in the most High [Elyon]?'
11.notes: The creed of practical atheism: not 'there is no God' but 'God is not watching' (cf. Psalm 10:11; 94:7). The taunt names Him Elyon (H5945), Most High, in the act of denying His deah (H1844) — rebellion that keeps the title and cancels the attributes.

12.text: Look — these are the wicked, always at ease, and they pile up wealth.
12.amp: Behold, these are the ungodly [rasha], who prosper [shalev — at ease] in the world [olam]; they increase [sagah] in riches [chayil].
12.notes: The exhibit summarized: shalev (H7961), untroubled ease, as a permanent address — olam — and chayil (H2428) compounding. Asaph's file on the defense closes; his own cross-examination begins.

13.text: Surely it was for nothing that I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence,
13.amp: Verily I have cleansed [zakah] my heart [lebab] in vain [riq — for emptiness], and washed [rachats] my hands [kaph] in innocency [niqqayon].
13.notes: Envy's arithmetic reaches its conclusion: purity as a losing trade — zakah (H2135) for riq (H7385), the empty nothing of Psalm 2:1. The 'surely' mimics verse 1's: two rival creeds now stand, each claiming certainty.

14.text: for I have been struck with plagues all day long, and my chastening arrived every morning.
14.amp: For all the day [yom] long have I been plagued [naga], and chastened ['my chastisement was', tokachath, the KJV margin] every morning [boqer].
14.notes: The inversion completed: the naga (H5060) the wicked escaped (v. 5) lands on the clean-handed man, with tokachath (H8433) served at boqer like a standing appointment. The books, read from outside the sanctuary, appear to run exactly backward.

15.text: If I had said, 'I will talk like that,' I would have betrayed the generation of Your children.
15.amp: If I say [amar], 'I will speak [saphar] thus'; behold, I should offend [bagad — deal treacherously] against the generation [dor] of Your children [ben].
15.notes: What held the slipping man: pastoral responsibility. bagad (H898) is covenant treachery — to publish his doubt as doctrine would betray the dor of God's banim, the little ones watching him. Some things are true to feel and treason to preach; Asaph carried the question to the right room instead.

16.text: So I kept turning it over, trying to understand it, and it was wearying pain in my eyes,
16.amp: When I thought [chashab] to know [yada] this, it was too painful for me ['labour in mine eyes', amal be-ayin, the KJV margin];
16.notes: chashab (H2803), the reckoning-verb, run at full load and failing: the problem of the prosperous wicked is not computable from street level. amal (H5999) in the eyes — the very trouble-word of verse 5, now describing the cost of staring at it.

17.text: until I came into the sanctuary of God; then I understood their end.
17.amp: Until I went [bo] into the sanctuary [miqdash] of God [El]; then understood [bin] I their end [acharit — their latter end, their outcome].
17.notes: The psalm's hinge, and one of Scripture's great 'untils': what analysis could not produce, the miqdash (H4720) gave — perspective. bin (H995) arrives with the acharit (H319) in view: the wicked judged not by their present feed but by their final frame. Worship is where the ledger gets its last column back.

18.text: Surely You have set them on slippery ground; You cast them down into ruins.
18.amp: Surely You did set [shith] them in slippery places [chalaqot]: You cast them down [naphal] into destruction [mashshuah — ruins].
18.notes: The third 'surely' corrects the second: the footing Asaph envied is chalaqot (H2513), smooth ice — and set there by God's own shith (H7896). Asaph's feet almost slipped ON THE WAY DOWN to envy them; theirs are placed where slipping is the design.

19.text: How they become a desolation in a moment — finished, swept away completely by terrors!
19.amp: How are they brought into desolation [shammah], as in a moment [rega]! they are utterly consumed [suph tamam — ended, finished] with terrors [ballahah].
19.notes: The tempo of judgment: rega (H7281), one moment — decades of shalev ease, then shammah (H8047) between two breaths. suph and tamam (H5486, H8552) stack the completion-verbs: not damaged, ended, with ballahah (H1091), sudden dread, as the escort.

20.text: Like a dream when a man wakes up — so, O Lord, when You arise You will despise their shadow-image.
20.amp: As a dream [chalom] when one awakes [quts]; so, O Lord [Adonai], when You awake [ur — arise, rouse], You shall despise [bazah] their image [tselem — their shadow-form, their phantom].
20.notes: The definitive metaphor for wicked prosperity: a chalom (H2472) — vivid, urgent, and gone at quts (H6974), the waking. Their whole glittering estate is a tselem (H6754), a phantom-image with no substance behind it, and the divine waking dissolves it by mere bazah (H959), disregard.

21.text: When my heart was soured and grieved, and I was pierced through in my inmost self,
21.amp: Thus my heart [lebab] was grieved [chamets — soured, embittered], and I was pricked [shanan — pierced as by a sharpened point] in my reins [kilyah — my kidneys, my inmost being].
21.notes: The retrospective diagnosis, told with a chemist's word: chamets (H2556), leavened sour — envy as fermentation of the lebab. shanan (H8150) is the sharpening-verb of arrows: the bitterness ran needles through the kilyah (H3629), the same inmost place God once counseled him from (cf. Psalm 16:7).

22.text: I was brutish and knew nothing; I was a mere beast before You.
22.amp: So foolish [baar — brutish] was I, and ignorant ['I knew not', yada, the KJV margin]: I was as a beast [behemah] before ['with', im, the KJV margin] You.
22.notes: The verdict on his season of envy: baar (H1198), brute-stupid, a behemah (H929) — reasoning about providence at a grazing animal's altitude. Yet note the preposition the margin preserves: a beast WITH You — even at his most brutish, he never left the pasture of God's keeping.

23.text: Nevertheless — I am with You continually; You have taken hold of my right hand.
23.amp: Nevertheless I am continually [tamid] with You: You have holden [achaz — gripped fast] me by my right [yamin] hand [yad].
23.notes: The most magnificent 'nevertheless' in the Psalter: the beast-with-God discovers the WITH was mutual all along, tamid (H8548). And the grammar of security: not 'I held on' but achaz (H270) — YOU gripped MY yamin; the grip that survived the almost-slip of verse 2 was never his own (cf. Psalm 63:8).

24.text: With Your counsel You will guide me, and afterward You will receive me into glory.
24.amp: You shall guide [nachah] me with Your counsel [etsah], and afterward [achar] receive [laqach — take] me to glory [kabod].
24.notes: The whole pilgrimage in one line: nachah (H5148), the shepherd-verb, by etsah (H6098) now — and achar (H310), afterward, laqach (H3947), the taking-verb used of Enoch whom God took (cf. Genesis 5:24). The acharit of the wicked was ruin (v. 17); the afterward of the held man is kabod (H3519). The Old Testament rarely says heaven more plainly.

25.text: Whom have I in heaven but You? And beside You there is nothing on earth that I desire.
25.amp: Whom have I in heaven [shamayim] but You? and there is none upon earth [eretz] that I desire [chaphets] beside You.
25.notes: The psalm's summit, and envy's final cure: both realms surveyed — shamayim and eretz, the wicked man's claimed jurisdictions of verse 9 — and one Person found sufficient in each. chaphets (H2654): the desire that had leaked toward the prosperous wicked now gathered wholly home.

26.text: My flesh and my heart waste away and fail — but God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever.
26.amp: My flesh [sheer] and my heart [lebab] fail [kalah — are spent, consumed]: but God [Elohim] is the strength ['rock', tsur, the KJV margin] of my heart, and my portion [cheleq] forever [olam].
26.notes: kalah (H3615): the honest anthropology — sheer (H7607) and lebab both burn down like wicks. Against the failing, tsur lebabi (H6697): God as the rock OF the heart, bedrock under the very organ that fails, and cheleq le-olam (H2506) — the portion-word of Psalm 16:5 stamped with forever. The wicked had riches; Asaph has the estate.

27.text: For look: those who are far from You will perish; You put an end to everyone who leaves You in unfaithfulness.
27.amp: For, lo, they that are far [rachoq] from You shall perish [abad]: You have destroyed [tsamat] all them that go a whoring [zanah — are faithless] from You.
27.notes: The final ledger in covenant terms: distance itself is the death — rachoq (H7369) resolves to abad (H6). zanah (H2181) is the prophets' word for covenant adultery (cf. Hosea; James 4:4): the wicked of this psalm are not strangers but deserters, and desertion has one acharit.

28.text: But as for me — the nearness of God is my good. I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may recount all Your works.
28.amp: But it is good [tov] for me to draw near [qirbah — the nearness of God] to God [Elohim]: I have put [shith] my trust [machseh — refuge] in the Lord GOD [Adonai YHWH], that I may declare [saphar — recount] all Your works [melakah].
28.notes: The answer to verse 1 finally earned: God is good to Israel — and MY good, says Asaph, is qirbat Elohim (H7132), His nearness itself, not His payouts. machseh (H4268) chosen, shith (H7896), deliberately placed — and the purpose clause turns the whole ordeal to testimony: saphar (H5608), recounting all His works, this psalm being exhibit one.
